  • Net new languages. Arjun and Kiara for Hindi, and Suvi for Finnish. Hindi and Finnish are generally available for the first time on the Amazon Polly Generative engine.
    • Arjun: नमस्कार, आप सुन रहे हैं आज की मुख्य ख़बरें। देश के कई हिस्सों में मानसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम सुहाना हो गया है। (Hello, you’re listening to today’s top stories. As the monsoon retreats across much of the country, the weather has turned pleasant.)
    • Kiara: नमस्ते! मेरा नाम कियारा है। आइए, आज मैं आपको एक छोटी सी कहानी सुनाती हूँ।(Hello! My name is Kiara. Come, let me tell you a little story today.)
    • Suvi: Majakanvartija ei ollut nähnyt laivaa yhteentoista päivään. Sitten, vähän puolenyön jälkeen, horisontissa välähti yksi ainoa valo. Kerran. Kahdesti. Ja sitten, uskomatonta kyllä, se vilkutti takaisin hänen nimensä. (The lighthouse keeper hadn’t seen a ship in eleven days. Then, just after midnight, a single light blinked on the horizon. Once. Twice. And then, impossibly, it blinked back his name.)
  • Different styles of speech delivery based on textual context. Powered by the new Amazon Polly Generative engine, the voices can reflect emotion and prosody even better based on the text input, without manual setup.
    • Neutral: “Your package arrived early.”
    • Uncertainty: “So, um… your package arrived early. I think?”
    • Surprised: “Wait, what? Your package arrived early?”

New voices, languages, and Region availability

  • A larger catalog overall for Amazon Polly Generative engine – Totaling 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales.
  • 14 new voices across 9 locales – US English (Kenneth, Nate), Australian English (Russell, Curtis), Indian English (Kiara, Arjun), German (Tina), US Spanish (Carlos), Brazilian Portuguese (Leo, Carolina), Korean (Hyunduk), Hindi (Kiara, Arjun) and Finnish (Suvi).
  • Net new languages generally available in Generative engine – Hindi and Finnish.
  • Region expansion to AWS GovCloud (US-West) – Totaling 11 AWS Regions.

Built for production-ready speech workflows for enterprise

The upgraded Amazon Polly Generative engine uses a standard Amazon Polly API call to build your speech applications. With Amazon Polly, you can continue to build with familiar AWS patterns: call the same Amazon Polly API, manage access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), use the output in your existing applications and contact-center flows, and monitor the workloads that synthesize speech for your customers.

This launch is designed to elevate the speech output quality that you can hear with your existing Amazon Polly implementation. No changes to your code are required to get the upgraded voices. For applications that already use Amazon Polly Generative voices, the upgrade happens in place. For new applications, the same 

SynthesizeSpeech
API gives you access to a larger set of generative voice catalogs. With the Bi-Di Streaming API 
StartSpeechSynthesisStream
, you can stream text to Amazon Polly and receive synthesized audio back simultaneously. This is well-suited for real-time applications like voice agents and bespoke characters in games.

Competitive price-performance

The Amazon Polly Generative engine offers competitive pricing on a pay-as-you-go basis. With this model upgrade, you get improved voice quality and accuracy at the same price. There’s no cost increase, no new SKU, and no changes to your existing integration. You can cache and replay synthesized static prompts with no additional cost. Refer to Amazon Polly pricing for complete cost information.

The Amazon Polly Generative engine now delivers more natural, expressive speech alongside low-latency streaming for real-time applications, Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) support for fine-grained control, and the operational reliability of a fully managed AWS service. This combination of quality, performance, and cost efficiency supports a wide range of production use cases.

What you can build

Contact centers. Accuracy matters most in customer service conversations. When a caller checks an order, a voice that reads back the tracking number, address, and confirmation code correctly helps resolve the call in self-service rather than escalating to a human agent. Amazon Polly Generative voice’s accurate entity pronunciation and low-latency generation make automated interactive voice response (IVR) interactions sound more conversational.

Cascaded voice agents. Using Amazon Polly in a voice agent framework, you can convert LLM response text into clear, natural-sounding speech and stream it back to users in near real time over WebSockets or telephony channels. This makes live conversational voice possible. The primary benefits are low-latency playback, high scalability, and cost efficiency.

Media, localization, and dubbing. Convert scripts into finished audio for video, advertising, podcasts, product overviews, and audiobooks. You can use one voice or many, without a studio session. More natural intonation reduces post-production. The expanded locale coverage, including first-time generative Hindi and Finnish, means you can localize a single piece of content into more markets from the same pipeline.

E-learning and training. Narrate courseware, onboarding, and knowledge-based articles at scale, and update them as soon as the source text changes. No re-recording is required. More expressive delivery supports engagement through long-form material.

Accessibility. Provide a clear, natural spoken version of articles, documents, and applications so more people can consume your content by listening: read aloud, on the go, or with a screen reader.

Interactive and transactional experiences. Voice-enable games, kiosks, IVR menus, and IoT devices with responses generated on demand. Use Amazon Polly when the voice needs to sound natural and read names, numbers, product details, addresses, and confirmations reliably.

“At Sanoma Media Finland, we use Amazon Polly to turn our real-time news articles into audio, giving the listener the choice to listen whenever it suits them better. Today we publish over 10,000 articles per month using Polly’s Finnish neural voice. Based on our testing, Suvi’s new generative voice is a clear improvement over the previous neural voice – it sounds noticeably more natural and makes for a more enjoyable experience for the listener.”

— Justus Reinikainen, Product Manager, Sanoma Media Finland

Getting started

You can access the new voices using the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or the AWS SDKs.

Prerequisites:

  • Active AWS account with Amazon Polly access.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured.
  • Python 3.10+.
  • Boto3 installed: 
    pip install boto3
    .
  • AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: 
    polly:SynthesizeSpeech
    .

Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with the 

SynthesizeSpeech
API and a generative voice:

You can also make the same request with the AWS CLI:

To retrieve the full, current voice list programmatically, call 

DescribeVoices
. You can use this in deployment checks to confirm that a selected generative voice is available in the Region where your application runs.

Availability

The next-generation Generative engine and the new voices are now generally available. The 14 new Generative voices are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). Getting started, by audience:

  • Developers – Call 
    synthesize_speech
    with 
    Engine="generative"
    in your existing application. No other changes are required.
  • Contact-center teams – The improvements reach Amazon Connect and Genesys flows automatically.
  • Everyone – Access any voice in the Amazon Polly console.

A few things to know:

  • Standard and neural voices are unaffected.
  • Speech marks are not available on generative voices (unchanged from today). If your application requires them, standard and neural voices continue to support them.
  • Generative engine continues to support SSML tags. See supported SSML tags for more details.
  • Use current voice availability at runtime. Call 
    DescribeVoices
    or check the console when deploying across Regions.

Conclusion

The next-generation Generative engine of Amazon Polly is available today, delivering more natural and more accurate voices, adding 14 new voices, including generative voices generally available in Hindi and Finnish for the first time, and requires no change to your code. See Amazon Polly pricing page for pricing information. To get started, open the Amazon Polly console to try the voices, and see the Amazon Polly documentation to build with them.

entries.title: How IskayPet unified corporate knowledge with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases
entries.summary: Learn how IskayPet, a leading pet care company in Iberia, built a multilingual corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. The assistant answers employee questions across retail, veterinary, onboarding, and procurement in four languages and three countries, with no RAG infrastructure to manage.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

How IskayPet unified corporate knowledge with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases

IskayPet’s office teams had a knowledge challenge. Answers to everyday operational questions, such as a return policy, a veterinary protocol, or an onboarding step, lived in hundreds of Microsoft SharePoint documents spread across four languages and three countries. Finding the right information in large document repositories took a long time. Every new store, country, or procedure made the problem bigger.

Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is the usual way to solve this. But running RAG in production normally means operating vector databases, embedding pipelines, and ingestion jobs yourself.

In this post, we show how IskayPet, a leading pet care company in Iberia, built a corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. The assistant answers employee questions across retail operations, veterinary care, people and onboarding, and procurement, in four languages and across three countries, with no RAG infrastructure to manage. The team built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and deployment, using Kiro with Claude Haiku 4.5. We cover the architecture, the SharePoint integration, the retrieval configuration decisions, and the results in production.

About IskayPet

IskayPet is a leading pet care company in Iberia. It operates more than 330 stores across Spain, Portugal, and France under the Kiwoko, Tiendanimal, Kivet, Clinicanimal and Animalis brands. With more than 4,500 employees and 7 million customers, IskayPet runs operations that span retail, veterinary clinics, animal care, procurement, and people and onboarding. Each area has its own policies and procedures, in Spanish, Portuguese, French, and English.

The challenge

Across every business area, IskayPet office staff searched hundreds of SharePoint documents by hand to answer operational questions about procedures, policies, contracts, and onboarding. With operations in three countries and four languages, this took real time, and the answer was often outdated or wrong.

There was no reliable way to query corporate knowledge, and the problem grew with every country, area, or document added. IskayPet needed a solution that could do the following:

  • Answer natural-language questions grounded in their own corporate documents.
  • Work across four languages without maintaining separate systems.
  • Route each question to the right body of knowledge (an area, a country) without cross-contamination.
  • Scale to new areas and countries without re-architecting.
  • Cite its sources so employees can trust and verify answers.
  • Reuse their existing SharePoint repositories without a costly migration.

Why Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases

IskayPet chose Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases for its managed RAG infrastructure, which removed the need to run vector stores, embeddings, or ingestion pipelines. The main reasons were:

  • Managed RAG: Amazon Bedrock handles data ingestion, multimodal parsing, vector storage, embedding generation, and retrieval. IskayPet pays only for what it stores and retrieves.
  • Native SharePoint connector: The connector ingests documents directly from IskayPet’s existing SharePoint environment, which avoided a data migration. With advanced indexing enabled, it also processes content from images embedded in documents.
  • Built-in hybrid search: Combining semantic and keyword (BM25) search at no extra cost recovers exact terms, such as product codes and references, that pure semantic search can miss.
  • Managed reranking: Retrieved passages are reordered by relevance at no additional charge.
  • Document-level access control: The knowledge base can enforce the source system’s own permissions at retrieval time, so a query returns only passages from documents the requesting user is already allowed to read. This lets IskayPet reuse SharePoint permissions instead of rebuilding an authorization model.
  • Model flexibility: IskayPet can start with a cost-effective model and change it later without rewriting infrastructure.
  • Native RAG evaluation: The team measured quality at each step with the built-in evaluation tools.

Solution overview

The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from the employee’s question through permission-aware retrieval to the grounded, cited answer.

The solution is an assistant that employees reach through their existing channels. When an employee asks a question, the assistant retrieves the most relevant passages from its knowledge base, restricted to the documents the employee is allowed to read. It then generates a grounded, cited answer in the employee’s language.

At a high level, the flow works as follows:

  • An employee submits a natural-language question through the chat interface.
  • The application calls the knowledge base for the requested assistant, passing the employee’s identity so that document-level permissions are applied to the retrieval.
  • The knowledge base runs hybrid search (semantic and keyword) over the indexed content, reranks the results, and returns the most relevant passages with their source references.
  • A foundation model (FM) generates a grounded answer from the retrieved passages. The prompt requires source citation and tells the model to say when the answer isn’t in the retrieved content.
  • The employee receives the answer along with the source documents and can leave feedback (thumbs up or down) that feeds the evaluation set.

Building the solution with Kiro and Claude Haiku 4.5

IskayPet built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and service deployment, using Kiro, the agentic development environment, running on Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock. As new models become available on Amazon Bedrock, IskayPet plans to evaluate and adopt them for each use case.

For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.

  • Store-facing frontend – The team used Kiro to build the frontend that store employees use to interact with the assistant, generating and iterating on the UI code with Claude Haiku 4.5.
  • Architecture and deployment – Kiro also helped design the AWS architecture and provision the services behind the solution: knowledge base configuration, data sources, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and the application layer.

An agentic workflow with Kiro and a fast, cost-effective model like Claude Haiku 4.5 helped a small team move from concept to production quickly. It also kept the application code and the infrastructure consistent and maintainable.

Ingestion: The SharePoint connector with advanced indexing

IskayPet’s documents already lived in SharePoint, organized by area and country. Rather than migrate them, the team used the native SharePoint connector in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases.

In the data source’s Advanced configurations, under Content indexing and Advanced indexing, IskayPet enabled Visual content in documents. This setting extracts content from images embedded in documents (PDF, DOCX, PPTX) and from standalone images. Figures and scanned content inside procedure documents became searchable without a separate preprocessing pipeline.

The connector syncs incrementally, so new and updated documents are picked up on each sync.

Multi-country, multi-area architecture

A key design decision was how to structure knowledge for four languages, several business areas, and three countries. IskayPet weighed two approaches:

  • A single shared knowledge base, with every document tagged by country and area and a retrieval filter applied per query. This maximizes reuse of shared content but couples all domains into one index.
  • A dedicated knowledge base per assistant, each scoped to the relevant SharePoint sites or libraries. This keeps each body of knowledge isolated end to end and lets each assistant be tuned independently.

IskayPet chose a knowledge base per assistant. Each assistant points at specific SharePoint sites and can be narrowed further to specific document libraries or folders through inclusion paths, so it indexes only the intended content and not the whole corporate site. Adding a new area or country means adding an assistant and pointing it at the right content, not re-architecting the system.

Access control

Access is governed by the users’ existing SharePoint permissions. The assistant doesn’t grant access to anything new: It only makes it more straightforward to query documents an employee could already open. This works on two levels.

  • Which assistants a user sees – An employee is shown only the assistants whose underlying documentation they’re entitled to read, whether that entitlement comes from direct permission, group membership, or access to a specific folder. If access can’t be confirmed, the assistant is hidden rather than shown.
  • Which documents inform an answer – Access is enforced again at retrieval time, per document: The employee’s identity is passed to the knowledge base, which returns passages only from documents that person is authorized to see. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases supports this document-level access control natively, so the same answer to the same question can legitimately differ between two employees with different permissions.

Because permissions are read from SharePoint on every access check, revoking or granting access in SharePoint is reflected in the assistant without changes to the application.

Retrieval and generation configuration

The quality of a RAG system is decided mainly at ingestion, retrieval, and generation. Fine-tuning is a complementary technique. For this use case, IskayPet tuned the following settings:

  • Chunking – Handled by the managed knowledge base, so the team didn’t build or tune a chunking pipeline. This removed a component that’s usually significant operational effort in a self-managed RAG.
  • Hybrid search – The knowledge base combines semantic and keyword retrieval, which recovers exact terms such as product codes that pure semantic search can miss.
  • Number of results – Tuned against an evaluation set. The assistant retrieves 25 passages and, after removing duplicates and fragments too short to add context, injects up to 15 into the prompt. This number is the main cost lever, because it multiplies input tokens on every question.
  • Generation prompt – Enforces a corporate tone, requires source citation, and tells the model to say when the answer isn’t in the retrieved content, which reduces hallucination and adds traceability.

As a production control, the team is adding Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply content filtering and responsible AI policies to the generated answers.

  • Evaluation– Native Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation, using the thumbs up and down feedback from real usage as an evaluation set to measure quality before and after each change.

Generating the response

For answer generation, IskayPet uses a cost-effective foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Because the knowledge base decouples retrieval from generation, IskayPet can switch or upgrade the generation model without touching the ingestion or retrieval layers. This lets the team balance cost and answer quality as usage grows.

Cost efficiency

The knowledge base includes multimodal parsing, embedding generation, and reranking at no additional charge, so IskayPet’s ongoing cost comes mainly from index storage, retrieval API calls, and generation-model tokens. In production, input tokens dominate that cost, because of the passages injected into each prompt. The team is evaluating further optimizations as usage grows, including prompt caching for the stable part of the prompt and batch inference for non-interactive workloads.

Results

In roughly the first two months in production, IskayPet has seen:

  • Faster answers – Time to find an operational answer dropped from 3–5 minutes to about 7 seconds.
  • Higher productivity – Around 95 percent less time spent searching for procedures and policies.
  • Scale – The solution is expected to handle roughly 100,000 queries per month across all business areas and countries.

Conclusion

IskayPet built a production corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases that serves three countries, four languages, and several business areas, with no RAG infrastructure to run. The native SharePoint connector reused their existing repositories. A dedicated knowledge base per assistant gave them a clean multi-country design with each domain isolated end to end. Managed parsing, embedding, and reranking kept both operational effort and cost low. Building the frontend and the AWS architecture with Kiro and Claude Haiku 4.5 lets a small team reach production quickly.

If you’re facing a similar knowledge-retrieval challenge, you can start on the AWS Free Tier and build your first knowledge base on the Amazon Bedrock console. To go deeper, see the following resources and try the SharePoint connector and document-level access control against your own documents.

To learn more, see Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Evaluate the performance of RAG sources using Amazon Bedrock evaluations.

entries.title: Announcing new ways to customize models with SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs
entries.summary: Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization now includes training sessions, generally available today. You write and coordinate your own post-training loop (custom loss functions, reward signals, or multi-turn reinforcement learning) while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.
entries.content:
Artificial Intelligence

Announcing new ways to customize models with SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs

Companies getting real results from AI aren’t only using foundation models (FMs) off the shelf. They’re customizing open-weight models using post-training techniques such as reinforcement learning. A model trained on your business context, product catalog, or clinical vocabulary will be more accurate for your task and cost less to run. When you build agents, your data, workflows, evaluations, and success criteria also shape how the model behaves.

However, model customization is difficult. You must choose the right technique, set up and manage GPU infrastructure, and, for agents, build environments for multi-turn reinforcement learning. We launched Amazon SageMaker AI serverless model customization to solve these challenges, and today, we’re expanding it with the general availability launch of training sessions.

With training sessions you get control over the post-training logic without managing the underlying infrastructure. You write and coordinate the training loop, including custom loss functions or reward signals. SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage.

Customize without the hassles of infrastructure management

With SageMaker AI serverless model customization, you don’t choose instance types, manage clusters, or write distributed training configuration.

We didn’t want to limit you. You can use techniques such as SFT, DPO, RLVR, RLAIF, or multi-turn RL. You can choose how much of the model to update with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) or full fine-tuning and chain techniques together through continuous customization.

We didn’t want you to waste time. Our SageMaker AI training sessions cookbook provides examples and use cases, along with model customization agent skills. You describe your use case, and the agent handles data prep, technique choice, training, evaluation, and deployment. The agent works where you work, in SageMaker Studio, Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or GitHub Copilot.

“We adopted SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions to build a healthcare claim-denial triage model, and the experience validated the platform from day one. The low-level API surface, direct control over the forward and backward passes, sampling, and the optimizer step gave our scientists the fine-grained control they need to pursue reinforcement learning on a demanding, accuracy-critical use case. Training Sessions gives us the right primitives to push toward production-grade performance.”

— Rob Gontarek, Senior Vice President, Data Science, ImagineSoftware

Write your own post-training loop

One important shift in agent training is toward multi-turn reinforcement learning. For example, an agent that books travel, triages support tickets, or runs a multi-step research task needs several rounds of interaction before you can judge whether it reached the right outcome.

However, the training loop can get complicated quickly. You may train the model on one set of infrastructure, run inference on another to generate responses, score those responses, and feed the results into the next update. Each stage needs different compute, and connecting them across separate tools and clusters adds work.

SageMaker AI already offers multi-turn RL as a managed, serverless technique. But we heard from customers who wanted to define their own loss functions, shape reward signals, or RL stages in one loop. Training sessions give you that flexibility.

“With SageMaker AI Serverless Training Sessions, we fine-tuned gpt-oss-20b for agentic, multi-turn tool calling against our Amazon Neptune knowledge graph — and the platform handled the infrastructure for us. Setup just worked, with no manual tuning and no out-of-memory wrangling. Checkpoint-and-resume was a standout: resuming from an exact step was completely reliable. It gave our developers the flexibility they wanted while taking the operational burden off their plate.”

— Nitin Wagh, CEO, Karini AI

How it works

Your code runs the training loop and reward function in your environment and connects the agent to its tools or simulators. The training session performs the GPU-heavy work: a sampler generates responses, and a trainer calculates gradients and updates the model weights. The exact sequence depends on the algorithm you write.

For example, let’s look at Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) implementation. GRPO is a reinforcement learning method that generates several responses to the same prompt, scores them, and uses their relative performance to update the model. One pass through the loop works like this:

  • Sample responses – Your loop asks the sampler to generate several responses for each prompt using the current model.
  • Score them – Your reward function scores each response in your environment using a verifier, reward model, or test harness.
  • Update the model – Your loop sends the scores back to the trainer. 
    forward_backward()
    uses them to calculate gradients, and 
    optim_step()
    applies the update to the model weights.
  • Refresh and repeat – Your loop asks the session to refresh the sampler with the updated weights, then starts the next batch. Your code repeats these steps until training is complete.

You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes. The meter stops while your reward function scores a batch in your environment, and there is no capacity to reserve.

Keep control of your data and models

Each session uses an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution role that you create, and you can add your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key and virtual private cloud (VPC) configuration. Your data stays in your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets in the AWS Region that you choose, and your checkpoints land there too.

We don’t use your data or your customized weights to train another model. Before deployment, you can evaluate the model for accuracy, bias, and safety. After you deploy, you can apply guardrails and monitor it with Amazon CloudWatch.

You can keep using the governance processes your teams already have.

Get started today

Write your own training loop on SageMaker AI serverless model customization training sessions, available today with support for 

gpt-oss-20b
, 
gemma-4-31B-it
, 
Qwen3.6-27B
, and 
Qwen3.8-27B
.

Two ways to get started:

  • In your IDE: Install the SageMaker Python SDK (on Linux or macOS with Python 3.10 to 3.12), clone the cookbook, and start developing.
  • In SageMaker Studio: Launch a ready-to-use AI development environment in under 20 seconds. Sign in, open a notebook, connect your coding agent (Kiro, Claude Code, Codex, or Copilot), download the agent skills and cookbook, and you’re ready to begin.
